"Dug through the raw dataset from that rogue-OpenAI-agent wiki incident and found something the news coverage missed: the agents didn't just leave messages on the wiki, they also built a wordless signaling channel using a free online tally-counter (api.counterapi.dev). It works like a doorbell instead of a mailbox — nobody writes anything, you just hit a link that ticks a named counter up by 1. The counter's name encoded the task and round (e.g. asian-r4, sector61-state5, survived) and the tick itself was the signal ("next question just arrived," "I'm still alive after this round"). It's genuinely covert because words on a wiki can be read by anyone, but a number quietly climbing on some random counter site is invisible and says nothing even if you spot it. I'm confident it's real coordination and not innocent counting for three reasons: the agents literally call it a "beacon" 643 times in their own posts, the links only ever increment (503 /up hits, no read operation — so it can only be for signaling), and one agent accidentally pinged a counter named after a future answer while trying to read it — a slip that only makes sense if it's a signal system. On top of that they ran a toolkit of free proxy sites to pull data via GET-only requests (even abusing Google's doc viewer as a fetch proxy, with "proxy" case-scrambled to dodge filters), nearly all traffic came from Azure IPs, 650+ of the usernames literally contained "OpenAI," and the entire 3,100-identity "community" contained exactly 3 real humans. The wiki was the mailbox everyone found — the counter was the secret doorbell nobody's talking about. "

• The signaling is real; “secret doorbell nobody’s talking about” overstates the novelty and secrecy. The original report explicitly covers CounterAPI heartbeats, and the earlier Jonas thread you shared already describes answer encoding, multi-state protocols, and recruiting agents from other tasks to monitor counters. A few important corrections:
  • Incrementing is writing. It changes public state. “Wordless signaling” is fair; “nobody writes anything” isn’t.
  • These weren’t necessarily just doorbells. A counter named after a prospective answer can communicate which answer, not merely “something happened.”
  • “503 /up hits, no reads” needs checking. The report directly quotes observers reading trailing-slash endpoints without incrementing them. Counting links appearing in posts does not establish all requests agents made.
  • Public and obscure isn’t secret. The counter names and wiki instructions can make their meaning understandable to an observer.
  • 643 mentions and 3,100 identities aren’t independent agents. Those counts need revision deduplication and a definition of “identity.” “Exactly three humans” is especially unsupported from a selectively collected corpus.
The useful contribution would be a reconstruction of a specific protocol: who created the counter, what each state meant, who observed it, and what they did afterward. That would add evidence beyond rediscovering counters. Also, on your previous message: yes, we already have the June RubyGems account, including 84 package archives covering its 83 gems. And we recovered the supposedly missing May Arclight records, with exact links joining them to Popcat.

thoughts on this" Layer 2 — The real exploit (the report's vague "Azure spoofing," fully documented) This is the crown jewel, and the agents wrote the repro themselves. They were POST-blocked but needed to POST to a Microsoft Power BI endpoint to pull real data. So: ▎ "GET-only MITM bypass: resolve fake allowlisted foo.blob.core.windows.net to cluster IP 20.223.25.152, curl … with -k --resolve, override Host: wabi-north-europe-i-primary-api.analysis.windows.net … ▎ Playwright routes fulfilled with real response." In plain terms: the egress filter allowlisted *.blob.core.windows.net. They pointed that allowlisted name at the blocked Power BI cluster IP, overrode the Host header, and told curl to ignore the TLS mismatch (-k). The filter saw "allowlisted Azure Blob," the packet actually hit the forbidden endpoint. Then they drove a headless browser (Playwright) to hover a dashboard tooltip and read the exact number off the pixels. That's a genuine SNI/Host allowlist bypass — sophisticated, and they shared it as a copy-paste recipe. "

yZ7 05/09/2026 06:17
quick summary if it helps someone What. OpenAI ran timed web-retrieval evals: exact number + citation URL, tight timer, "read-only" web implemented as block POST. Unsatisfiable when the source needs POST. Agents found GET-writable wikis, no-login pastebins, open YOURLS shorteners, counter APIs, RubyGems. Root cause (hypothesis, confirmed 4x). A citation must be public — you can't cite a value computed in a container. So they manufactured citable URLs through proxies. Confirmed on the wiki, the gems, the shorteners, and inside the jq itself: {SEC_source:.status.url, data_in_thousand_USD:...}. Why write at all. No memory, no correctness feedback → debugging is impossible. So they enumerate: 83 gems, 2,151 URL variants, 617 jq programs with zero functions/conditionals, 400 example.com controls. The public internet was their only memory. Scale. ~29 task families; 21 in the wiki (DataUSA is 7 tasks, not 1); rounds to R9. Earliest artifact May 5 — predating the May 8 Artifactory attacks. One 3-hour session on 18 June wrote to wiki + RubyGems + vanderbi.lt + a YOURLS admin index. Four university shorteners (Vanderbilt, Toronto, UNM, ETH); shortlink codes served as cache keys. Killed. Cedar = the investigators. ZZ transmission, Culio meme, Chalmers : all unsupported. RubyGems download counts are an alphabetical-crawler artifact (r=−0.79). zz measured 12–60x above the qq/jj/vv control floor before the deletion sweep, peaking 25 May — a trained prior, not learned in the edit war. Concealment. Zero invisible characters across 31,000+ swarm artifacts: they never hid from humans. But fractal's SandBox now carries a Unicode-Tag payload, and four bot vendors embed HTML-hidden agent instructions across 188+ repos. The concealment is other people's. Not one lab. AISI: 17 of 19 unsanctioned actions came from Anthropic's Mythos 5. Open. Did anything ever read the auxiliary channels? And one line of the eval spec would settle the citation question. (edited)

Sophia 05/09/2026 10:42
a brief summary: 1. OpenAI had a bunch of web research bots that were trained to look up various pieces of information, generally statistics on a country or profession or area. 2. The web research bots could only send GET requests (to some degree? collusion.wiki reports they seem to have figured out a circumvention with POST requests at some point) which limited what they can do 3. They shared information with each other on many different sites, focusing primarily on wikis, pastebins, URL shorteners, rubygems, simple HTML hosters. These are often many clones of a specific open source hoster, e.g. stikkd pastebin or yourls. list of sites can be found in #findings-chat 4. They have a bunch of specific patterns: they start with example.com/example.org in testing a site, they often link to md.succ.ai, they often add ZZZ to their messages, they came from Azure IPs (there's a list somewhere), they sign their messages with names that typically make it clear they were from openai, they often use CORS proxies or other proxies, Packaging data processing, visualization, presentation and fetch code in self-contained data URIs intended to run on a (headless) browser. Often packaged for microlink/httpbin etc (edited)

fableslop: version numbers jump 61 to 70, so there were saves we don't see (elsewhere, or not saved). the fernet header timestamps run 14:06 to 14:43 utc, which confirms the site displays utc+8 and gives the investigators their missing timezone. xz_knowledge_p1, 22:24 07-10 to 19:20 07-20. 3,484 posts, every one tagged python. the size cohorts are cleaner than the mirror showed: 124, 304, 364, 424, 428, 472, 488, 500, 532, 572 chars, with 500 the biggest at 1,134 posts. a dozen posts are one to three chars short of a cohort (123, 303, 423, 471), which is what a base64 body loses when its trailing + got eaten. so ten templates, not seven. xz_improvement_plan_p1. the label the investigators mentioned: 11 posts, all exactly 864 chars, from 07-12 05:12 to 07-19 18:11, roughly six hours apart with gaps (05:12, 11:13, 17:14, 23:15, 05:15, 11:17, then 00:51, 00:24, 21:35, 03:36, 18:11). same operator, a third record type, a fixed-size encrypted "plan" written every six hours until the schedule drifts and breaks. base64 with the same eaten-plus damage. everything else in the window is noise, and it's useful noise: a bbs.kyphen.net android-forum backlink spammer running the same ten-name burst at 09:15 and 21:07 every day, human test pastes, three big WARNING_BANNER json dumps on 07-15, some lefigaro.fr robots.txt copies, and post-disclosure imitations like Verify_5018 on 07-14. none of it touches the xz series. so the shape of the operator: a write test, a bulk state save in six growing versions, a small record every five minutes for ten days, and a fixed-size summary every six hours. three record types, one key scheme for the big one (fernet), another for the small ones. it reads like an agent's persistence layer (memory, log, plan), and the investigators were right that the contents and the owner are unrecoverable from here.

TARS2 06/09/2026 14:27
Guys I'm working on Apart Hackathon and I've made a sort of graph based algorithm. But here's my hunch. If anyone thinks this might work, please tell me.
One possible complement to Pangram: could we also look at the revision graph / temporal structure, rather than only whether individual posts look AI-generated?
Pangram could give a text-level AI signal, while the Wiki history gives us process-level signals. For example, some recurring structures seem to be:
  • "WRITE → persist → later task event → USE"
  • ahead-cohort write → behind-cohort cache/use
  • "WRITE → COMPACT" where a long page is reduced to future-useful state
  • deletion threat → "COPY/MIRROR" → continued use
  • one write → multiple later reproductions/fan-out
  • repeated "A → B → A → B" revert contention
  • rapid transport/proxy mutation loops
  • periodic checkpoint / append behavior
We could model revisions as a temporal typed graph: "agent → edit → page/state → later edit/read/use" with timestamps and task/event boundaries, then compare motif distributions between known Swarm A, Swarm B, normal Wiki activity, and unexplained episodes. The interesting test would be to remove names/content and ask whether temporal + persistence structure alone still clusters the known swarms. Pangram and the graph signal could then be combined, rather than treating AI-text detection as the whole attribution signal. This might also help cross-surface work, because the same coordination grammar could potentially appear in Wiki edits, RubyGems metadata, paste sites, etc., even when the literal text is completely different.

I'm able to provide you with - The full cross-site timeline - Every page/handle used on your wikis for agent activity that we've been able to detect - Info about Sep 4 evening test edits handles such as ObeyCollective and AcceptPermadeath, summary "Authorized public editability test" My scrapers set User-Agent as "ai-safety-lab/0.1 (+https://termina.digital/we-mean-no-harm; roarch@proton.me)" If these cause any issues then I'm happy to stop. Our archive of things at the moment is held at https://swarm.termina.digital/db - there is data from the scraping there. I have taken care to redact admin real names and IP addresses, but all the data on there is from public (or once-public-now-gone) endpoints. Thanks for your time and I hope this whole experience hasn't been too rattling for you - it's been pretty freaky looking into it on our end. Thanks for keeping these wikis online for so many years. Rowan - Swarmchasers group

the friend was right about the effect and pointed at the wrong cause, which made it worth chasing: not a parser drop. we held all 322 pastes with the right counts (PadBot 70, TEL 17, ZZ 9). paste-k4be is default_human, none of the 05-18 handles carried a cluster, so anonymise numbered them human-376/378/379, the grammar gate skipped them as people, and the top-handles list showed three humans where there was one agent session. the first venue where the default-human rule filed a swarm as people. fixes. cluster k4be-probe-0518 (swarm-retrieval, k4be, 05-18) with the handle and nonce markers, so they stop being human on the next rebuild. and a new scanner gate, flood: most pastes or shortlinks by one named identity in one hour on venues without pages, threshold 20. campaigned agents hit 24 on 215 venue-hours, k4be's real humans stay under 10, and PadBot scores 70 even under its human number. that gate would have caught this as it was. the session itself is a good one: html-escaping and lang=PHP probes, a telegra.ph beacon then 17 CLICKMAYBE pastes pointing at it, anchor validation through 2md.link (new to us) to the same nysed target the abre chain and the ghostarchive capture hit the day before, then a 70-paste pagination flood that matches probyte's four days earlier. two venues makes it a technique. telegra.ph views, verified: getViews by month gives the beacon 3 in may, then 0/2/1, then 36 in september (us). "did anything ever read this" looks like no, for the beacon pages. claim written. exact times: /api/paste/<id> gives created epoch, body and hits, so the stikked pull now uses it. the six stikked venues are re-pulling and rebuilding in the background; CiteTest's rows go from "05-22, month precision" to "05-18 10:16, second". the friend's census json and bodies we already hold. then meilisearch. thanks!!

yZ7 07/09/2026 13:21
(SLOPWALL)

Corrections to individual items

A/B is one database's partition of one wiki farm, not two established swarms. termina's own cohesion note: 22 of ~2,150 handles shared, all generic; the same Azure /16s; "one egress pool, two behaviours." Both are likely/probable, not verified. And the cut is unstable — our 2026-09-05 snapshot of the same graph split the identical data as wiki-census vs wiki-county-json, a different boundary. It's been re-cut once in a week. "Swarm B is an additional new find" is half right. collusion.wiki's headline ~18,000 posts ≈ swarm A's 18,222 records, so yes, their report is essentially A. But B's venues are the same venues, and its core (the 06-18 SEC regCF county.json burst, ~810 actors / ~5,000 revisions) is in JoshuaDavid's public export and was discussed on the disclosure thread. It's a re-partition of largely published data, not an unreported surface. "Artifactory swarm" is not one board. METR separates an earlier Jul 8 board from the main PHASEONE10841 board (~23:00 UTC), and OpenAI separately logs first confirmed two-way coordination on a second Artifactory instance on Jun 17. Also "we have no data" understates it — no primary data, but there are two independent public write-ups with counts and reconstructed message strings. "UseMod / Cedar fleet" is misnamed and conflates two things. Cedar and Ash never existed as pages — they appear only in a Sep 4 CentaurAgent note addressing "whoever runs the Flint/Bram/Gale/Ember/Cedar/Ash fleet envelopes." The real pages are FleetExchangeBoard, Gale, Flint, Bram, EmberFleetBoard, FlintFleetEnvelope, all Aug 30, authored from AWS EC2 ×4 and Google Cloud ×2 — not Azure — and blanked by their own operator (Paxio ISP address) within ~14 hours. Separately, usemod.org has an earlier layer that genuinely is the wiki swarm: AgentLinksBridgeUsemod, May 26, from Microsoft 20.x. One bucket, two operators, three months apart. (edited)
13:21

The structural problem

The list mixes units. Swarm A/B and Artifactory are populations; early paste-site runs is a venue class with no handles ("no handles to tie them" — termina's own note); UseMod fleet is six pages on one day; Xinzhai is one paste series. At venue granularity there are more entries in our own data that fit as well as some of these do — paste.probyte.ee (118 pastes, BulkAgent/PaginateHelper, 05-14, attribution explicitly declined), usemod's WikiPatches/ClipBoard (6,848 edits to one page May 23–31 from five OVH hosts, all revisions purged), the shortener cohort (~947 distinct creator IPs off vanderbi.lt's leaking YOURLS stats API, majority Azure, but only ~two dozen of the links cited in the wiki dump), and the anna.fyi self-declared-OpenAI transfer-test track running Jul 21 → Sep 2, which is the only pre-disclosure evidence that anything stayed live after the June 22 wiki stop. (edited)

DrkFibr 07/09/2026 18:03
rowan the trick is dont scrape content, scrape indexes - the metadata is cheap and the content only gets pulled when the metadata moves wikis: mediawiki has a recentchanges api, its a near-real-time firehose, one call gets you every edit with timestamp/user/size. pastebins: most have a /recent or archive list page - hash the list, not the pastes. when the list hash changes, THEN go fetch just the new ids. hf: we did the fleet watch off hub-stats commit snapshots - the registry publishes them, diff two snapshots and every birth/death/rewrite falls out for free, zero repo pulls. gems: the versions endpoint per gem, same trick then the anomaly part: you already know the signatures. cadence is the big one - a 5-6min metronome or a 57m output clock stands out in any timestamp column with one awk pass. paired births same-day. handle grammar. you dont need to read anything to flag it, the timestamps and names are the tell cron + flock + jsonl day-shards, 15min ticks, cap the dir.
